It's a topic of much discussion in the bodyweight world: how can we sufficiently challenge our lower bodies, which are capable of producing such huge amounts of force, without resorting to using heavy weights and a barbell? Pistol squats aren't a complete solution, and even if they were, they eventually grow too easy, and when they do so, it is tempting to simply add weight and continue doing them forever. But in doing so, we would lose the spirit of bodyweight exercise, of always finding new ways to push ourselves to heightened levels of strength and athleticism without using external weight as resistance. In doing so we would become merely unilateral powerlifters, and begin asking ourselves, why not just squat and deadlift and leg press and leg curl like everyone else is doing? Of course, not everyone could do that even if they wanted to, so for them it is a matter not of philosophy but of practicality, and thus of even greater importance.

To escape all this drudgery, I present to you one of the solutions I have come upon in my bodyweight journey- sprinting. It is an elegantly simple solution, indeed, it may be the most obvious one. For most of human history [you know, before people got the idea to lift heavy pieces of metal for fun] sprinting was 90% or more of the anaerobic lower body exercise any human ever did. Think about it, which was more likely for our ancestors- having to run away from a bear, or having to pick up a 400 lb rock? Because of this, it is a fairly complete lower body exercise in itself, certainly at least as complete as pistols are. If I were forced to pick only one leg exercise, it might be a tough decision, but sprinting would win out in the end, perhaps merely because I enjoy it more than other lower body exercises, but also because of the powerful anabolic effect I know it can have.

Yes, I did say anabolic. Rumors abound of running making a person skinny, but in truth only distance running has this effect. Sprinting has the exact opposite effect, and in fact has been shown in studies to boost testosterone and improve nutrient partitioning in favor of muscles. And sprinting does build muscle, in much the same way that heavy barbell squatting does. Both have the effect of bringing the muscles close to their point of failure in a brief period of time, thus signalling the body to grow more fast-twitch muscle fibers [the big, impressive looking ones] in the muscle groups used, to prepare itself for next time. This is really all you need to grow muscle, you could achieve the same thing with short-distance bicycle racing [google "track cyclists" for proof of this] or climbing a short sequence of extremely steep stairs [like in the exercise, step-ups]. It is still good to perform multiple movements, to work the muscles in different proportions as well as to ward off boredom, but the point remains.

The true beauty of sprinting as a hypertrophy exercise lies in it's ease of access [you just need a roughly 100m long patch of land, preferably grass, to protect your knees] and ease of progression [just run faster! alternately, sprint up a hill or use a parachute, although it's really not needed]. And now that I've [hopefully] shown you the benefits sprinting can have on you and your bodyweight training, and proven logically that it can indeed build muscle, I hope to show you how to best do it, and how to program it into your current bodyweight strength regimen for best results.

While reading this, keep in mind that I'm not a competitive sprinter or coach, and I'm only teaching you how to do this as a muscle-building bodyweight exercise. In fact, I'm pretty slow, relatively speaking, and because of my under 6' height and Western European, long-torso-short-legs genetics, I'm well aware that I'll always be outrun by most tall, thin, leggy black dudes in even moderately good shape. I'm accepting of this, and you should be too. A lot of people don't like to run because they feel they are slow. Don't be too self-conscious, and certainly don't disregard this perfectly good exercise just because you'll never be world class at it! It will put muscle on you, I promise!

Now, the first thing you should keep in mind while sprinting is that you're doing it as a strength exercise, and not as cardio or even HIIT. Think of each individual sprint as a set, and rest accordingly. This knowledge alone will do wonders for your muscle gains, as it will relieve you from attempting to keep rest times short, or God forbid, do something crazy like 20-10 tabata intervals. The specific rest time I recommend is the amount of time it takes you to walk back, slowly, to your starting position, but if you want you can take even longer than that and it won't hurt you any. Don't rest enough to cool down, but definitely rest enough to allow yourself to recover sufficiently that the next sprint won't suffer. This will vary from person to person but a slow walk back to your start point is a good general guideline.

The next important thing to remember is that volume is your best friend, and your worst enemy. Volume in this case meaning the total distance sprinted in the session. You want to have enough volume to create a demand on your body for more muscle in your legs, but not so much volume that your sprints at the end of the session suffer and aren't really sprints, or the whole thing turns into a cardio session. I recommend building volume up to 10 x 100 meters, and then keeping it there, and only focusing on speed after that. This is enough to stimulate growth but not enough to trash your muscles completely. You can do the buildup by doing 10 x 50 meters at first and then increasing the distance by 5 meters every other session, or by doing 3-5 100 meter sprints and trying to increase the number every few sessions. Either method will work just fine. Important to keep in mind, though, is that, if at any point during your session your sprints stop feeling like sprints and start feeling more like trudges, stop. Pushing past point this won't get you any gains and will only serve to sabotage your efforts.

Now for how to sprint. The whole process is pretty natural, but there are some important things to keep in mind, especially if you haven't done it in awhile. First of all, when you first push off, you will lean forwards in order to accelerate faster. This is good, but you shouldn't stay in this position the whole time. Once you've reached full speed, come up out of the lean to stand upright and maintain speed to the finish. Secondly, DON'T reach forward in your strides. Keep your legs under you. It might seem like reaching forward would make you faster, but it won't, it will only put you at risk for injuring yourself. Now that you've got that, though, you SHOULD focus on "pulling" yourself over the ground with your hamstrings. This will allow you to engage them more and focus less on pushing off with your quads. Most people are heavily quad-dominant, but sprinting, by nature, should be a glute and hamstring dominant exercise. FInally, do pump your arms while you sprint. You can't hit max speed with your hands in your pockets.

Now a bit about programming. I recommend sprinting at the end of your calisthenics session, preferably after a low-rep strength session with a quad dominant exercise like pistols or shrimp squats. The reason for this is how these exercises, done for low reps, psych up your nervous system and allow you to sprint faster than you otherwise would be able to. If you don't believe me, try sprinting after a simple warmup, and then, a couple weeks later, sprinting after a warmup and maybe 5 x 3 of pistol squats, or a variation thereof. The difference will amaze you. This kind of programming also saves you from having to schedule a whole day for sprinting, which is a welcome relief for the busy bodyweight exerciser.

One more thing about speed- if you don't have well-developed glutes and hamstrings already, sprinting will immediately start fixing that by building some good lean muscle for you. However, if you're like me when I first started sprinting and you already have well-developed glutes and hamstrings from doing a different exercise like glute-ham raises or bridge curls, your initial gains will be purely neurological. What I mean by this is that you'll see dramatic jumps in speed almost immediately, but it won't be from muscle gain, it will just be your mind playing catch up to what your muscles are already capable of. If this sounds like you, consider doing some of your initial sprint sessions on a slight decline. This will help your mind catch up and help you realize your true speed faster, so that you can start getting muscle gains from sprinting sooner rather than later.

Well, that's about all I have to say about that. I hope I've taught you something about this great alternative bodyweight exercise, and given you some new ideas for lower body training. Demonic_Mime, out.

I prefer not talking about the 'spirit' of bodyweight exercise. Spirit is an ill defined characteristic with different interpretations, I'd prefer to say 'advantages', but that's a personal choice, I'm only mentioning it as you aim to become this sub's mod; also I wouldn't want this sub to sound anti-weights (i.e. "we only like pure bodyweight routines here"), but I know where you're coming from.

I'd suggest to use time (in seconds) as the measure of a set, in addition to measuring distance; as you get stronger/faster, you'll be able to go through the same distance in less time, but that might imply less volume as suggested here. So for example, if a single rep is equal to a time under tension of 5 seconds as suggested here, a person might first run for 25 seconds (5 reps) and record the distance traveled, then target to add 5 seconds every workout if they are 'adding reps', but if you want to keep it at 5x5 then just add 1/5th of the distance in the same amount of seconds.

Then again I have near-zero experience with sprinting, so maybe your approach is better, but it seems as if that's the approach you'd take to get better at a sprinting competition, not necessarily at strength or hypertrophy, even though you'd still build strength/hypertrophy with the 'only track distance' approach.

If you're doing strength training, you'd generally want to rotate your exercises; keeping sprinting for last sounds like a recipe to advance less at sprinting in relationship with the other exercises, because you'd be tired; you mention 'psyching up your nervous system', but isn't that what warm ups are for? Personally, I find that if I can perform an exercise better after adding something to my warm up, then it means that I didn't warm up enough.

Of course, I had no intention to offend weightlifters. But I do think bodyweight has a certain spirit of creativity to it that you don't get with weights. This is of course the same thing that some might see a disadvantage in, if they're so inclined, the convolutedness progressing sometimes has, and having to get to know your body in order to do so past a certain point. I just prefer to look at it as a feature and not a drawback, that's all.

I don't think your idea is a bad one, but keep in mind that volume in sprinting is measured in distance, not time, as it is simply the more objective and practical measurement. Although I'm sure your method would work just fine, every book and article I've ever read [even those aimed directly at hypertrophy] on the topic have done it similarly to the method I'm using, so I don't see why I'd reverse years of work and fix something that isn't broken.

I recommend doing your sprint training after your main workout for two reasons. One, it makes it easier to fit in your program. People are more likely to include sprint training if they don't have to schedule an entire separate workout day for it. Two, I really believe it improves performance, if you do it right. The key is doing them after the right exercise [shrimp squats or pistols work well] and doing that exercise for fairly low reps. Doing them after a quad dominant movement is especially beneficial as it forces you to engage your glutes and hamstrings more than you otherwise would. I like to do 5x3 for the movement, and any upper body exercise earlier in the session is mostly irrelevant. Strength training shouldn't really tire you out, in the same sense that a long run would.
